{{Short description|Influence on an oscillating physical system which reduces or prevents its oscillation}}
{{about|damping in oscillatory systems}}
{{Dynamics}}
[[File:Damped spring.gif|thumb|upright|Underdamped [[spring–mass system]] with {{nowrap|''ζ'' < 1}}]]

In [[physical system]]s, '''damping''' is the loss of [[energy]] of an [[oscillating system]] by [[dissipation]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Escudier |first1=Marcel |last2=Atkins |first2=Tony |date=2019 |title=A Dictionary of Mechanical Engineering |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1093/acref/9780198832102.001.0001 |website=Oxford Reference |doi=10.1093/acref/9780198832102.001.0001|isbn=978-0-19-883210-2 |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |author=Steidel |title=An Introduction to Mechanical Vibrations |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |year=1971 |page=37 |quote=''damped'', which is the term used in the study of vibration to denote a dissipation of energy}}</ref> Damping is an influence within or upon an oscillatory system that has the effect of reducing or preventing its oscillation.<ref>{{cite journal
 | last = Crandall | first = S. H.
 | date = January 1970
 | doi = 10.1016/s0022-460x(70)80105-5
 | issue = 1
 | journal = Journal of Sound and Vibration
 | pages = 3–18, IN1
 | title = The role of damping in vibration theory
 | volume = 11| bibcode = 1970JSV....11....3C
 }}</ref> Examples of damping include [[viscous damping]] in a fluid (see [[Viscosity|viscous]] [[Drag (physics)|drag]]), [[Friction|surface friction]], [[radiation]],<ref name=":1" /> [[Electrical resistance and conductance|resistance]] in [[electronic oscillators]], and absorption and scattering of light in [[optical oscillator]]s. Damping not based on energy loss can be important in other oscillating systems such as those that occur in [[ecology|biological systems]] and [[Bicycle and motorcycle dynamics#Lateral motion theory|bikes]]<ref name="MPRS">{{cite journal
| journal = [[Proceedings of the Royal Society A]]
| volume = 463
| issue = 2084
| year = 2007
| pages = 1955–1982
| title = Linearized dynamics equations for the balance and steer of a bicycle: a benchmark and review
| doi = 10.1098/rspa.2007.1857
| quote = lean and steer perturbations die away in a seemingly damped fashion. However, the system has no true damping and conserves energy. The energy in the lean and steer oscillations is transferred to the forward speed rather than being dissipated.
|bibcode = 2007RSPSA.463.1955M
|author1=J. P. Meijaard |author2=J. M. Papadopoulos |author3=A. Ruina |author4=A. L. Schwab  | s2cid = 18309860
|name-list-style=amp }}</ref> (ex. [[Suspension (mechanics)]]). Damping is not to be confused with [[friction]], which is a type of dissipative force acting on a system. Friction can cause or be a factor of damping.

Many systems exhibit oscillatory behavior when they are disturbed from their position of [[static equilibrium]]. A mass suspended from a spring, for example, might, if pulled and released, bounce up and down. On each bounce, the system tends to return to its equilibrium position, but overshoots it. Sometimes losses (e.g. frictional) damp the system and can cause the oscillations to gradually decay in amplitude towards zero or [[attenuation|attenuate]].

The '''damping ratio''' is a [[dimensionless]] measure, amongst other measures, that characterises how damped a system is. It is denoted by {{mvar|ζ}} ("[[zeta]]") and varies from '''undamped''' ({{math|1=''ζ'' = 0}}), '''underdamped''' ({{math|''ζ'' < 1}}) through '''critically damped''' ({{math|1=''ζ'' = 1}}) to '''overdamped''' ({{math|''ζ'' > 1}}).

The behaviour of oscillating systems is often of interest in a diverse range of disciplines that include [[control engineering]], [[chemical engineering]], [[mechanical engineering]], [[structural engineering]], and [[electrical engineering]]. The physical quantity that is oscillating varies greatly, and could be the swaying of a tall building in the wind, or the speed of an [[electric motor]], but a normalised, or non-dimensionalised approach can be convenient in describing common aspects of behavior.

==Oscillation cases==
[[File:Types of damping.webm|thumb|300px|Movement of the needle of a mechanical [[weighing scale]] when the mass-spring system within is underdamped, overdamped and critically damped. Critical damping is ideal for this device, because it minimises the time taken for the needle to settle, allowing a reading to be taken sooner.]]
Depending on the amount of damping present, a system exhibits different oscillatory behaviors and speeds.
* Where the spring–mass system is completely lossless, the mass would oscillate indefinitely, with each bounce of equal height to the last. This hypothetical case is called ''undamped''.
* If the system contained high losses, for example if the spring–mass experiment were conducted in a [[viscous]] fluid, the mass could slowly return to its rest position without ever overshooting. This case is called ''overdamped''.
* Commonly, the mass tends to overshoot its starting position, and then return, overshooting again. With each overshoot, some energy in the system is dissipated, and the oscillations die towards zero. This case is called ''underdamped.''
* Between the overdamped and underdamped cases, there exists a certain level of damping at which the system will just fail to overshoot and will not make a single oscillation. This case is called ''critical damping''. The key difference between critical damping and overdamping is that, in critical damping, the system returns to equilibrium in the minimum amount of time.<ref>{{cite book|title=College Physics|first1=Paul Peter|last1=Urone|first2=Roger|last2=Hinrichs|publisher=OpenStax|via=University of Central Florida|year=2016|contribution=16.7 Damped Harmonic Motion|contribution-url=https://pressbooks.online.ucf.edu/algphysics/chapter/damped-harmonic-motion/}}</ref>

==Damped sine wave==
{{distinguish|Damped wave (radio transmission)}}
[[File:DampedCosine.svg|thumb|350px|Plot of a damped sinusoidal wave represented as the function <math>y(t) = e^{- t} \cos(2 \pi t)</math>]]

A '''damped sine wave''' or '''damped sinusoid''' is a [[Sine wave|sinusoidal function]] whose amplitude approaches zero as time increases. It corresponds to the ''underdamped'' case of damped second-order systems, or underdamped second-order differential equations.<ref>Douglas C. Giancoli (2000). [''Physics for Scientists and Engineers with Modern Physics (3rd Edition)'']. Prentice Hall. p. 387 {{ISBN|0-13-021517-1}}</ref>
Damped sine waves are commonly seen in [[science]] and [[engineering]], wherever a [[harmonic oscillator]] is losing [[energy]] faster than it is being supplied.
A true sine wave starting at time = 0 begins at the origin (amplitude = 0). A cosine wave begins at its maximum value due to its phase difference from the sine wave. A given sinusoidal waveform may be of intermediate phase, having both sine and cosine components. The term "damped sine wave" describes all such damped waveforms, whatever their initial phase.

The most common form of damping, which is usually assumed, is the form found in linear systems. This form is exponential damping, in which the outer envelope of the successive peaks is an exponential decay curve. That is, when the maximum points of each successive curve are connected, the result resembles an exponential decay function. The general equation for an exponentially damped sinusoid may be represented as:
<math display="block">y(t) = A e^{-\lambda t} \cos(\omega t - \varphi)</math>
where:
*<math>y(t)</math> is the instantaneous amplitude at time {{mvar|t}};
*<math>A</math> is the initial amplitude of the envelope;
*<math>\lambda</math> is the decay rate, in the reciprocal of the time units of the independent variable {{mvar|t}};
*<math>\varphi</math> is the phase angle at {{math|1=''t'' = 0}};
*<math>\omega</math> is the [[angular frequency]].

Other important parameters include:
* [[Frequency]]: <math>f = \omega / (2\pi)</math>, the number of cycles per time unit. It is expressed in inverse time units <math>t^{-1}</math>, or [[hertz]].
* [[Time constant]]: <math>\tau = 1 / \lambda</math>, the time for the amplitude to decrease by the factor of ''[[e (mathematical constant)|e]]''.
* [[Half-life]] is the time it takes for the exponential amplitude envelope to decrease by a factor of 2. It is equal to <math>\ln(2) / \lambda</math> which is approximately <math>0.693 / \lambda</math>.
* Damping ratio: <math>\zeta</math> is a non-dimensional characterization of the decay rate relative to the frequency, approximately <math>\zeta = \lambda / \omega</math>, or exactly <math>\zeta = \lambda / \sqrt{\lambda^2 + \omega^2} < 1</math>.
* [[Q factor]]: <math>Q = 1 / (2 \zeta)</math> is another non-dimensional characterization of the amount of damping; high ''Q'' indicates slow damping relative to the oscillation.

== Damping ratio ==
[[File:2nd Order Damping Ratios.svg|thumb|400px|upright=1.3|The effect of varying damping ratio on a second-order system.]]

The ''damping ratio'' is a dimensionless parameter, usually denoted by ''ζ'' (Greek letter zeta),<ref>{{cite book
| title = Introduction to Mechatronics and Measurement 
| last = Alciatore
| first = David G.
| publisher = McGraw Hill
| year = 2007
| edition = 3rd
| isbn = 978-0-07-296305-2}}</ref> that characterizes the extent of damping in a second-order ordinary [[differential equation]]. It is particularly important in the study of [[control theory]]. It is also important in the [[harmonic oscillator]]. The greater the damping ratio, the more damped a system is.
*''Undamped'' systems have a damping ratio of 0.
*''Underdamped'' systems have a value of less than one.
*''Critically damped'' systems have a damping ratio of 1.
*''Overdamped'' systems have a damping ratio greater than 1.

The damping ratio expresses the level of damping in a system relative to critical damping and can be defined using the damping coefficient:

:<math> \zeta = \frac{c}{c_c} = \frac {\text{actual damping}} {\text{critical damping}},</math>

The damping ratio is dimensionless, being the ratio of two coefficients of identical units.

Taking the simple example of a [[mass-spring-damper model]] with mass ''m'', damping coefficient ''c'', and [[spring constant]] ''k'', where <math>x</math> represents the [[Degree of freedom (mechanics)|degree of freedom]], the system's [[equation of motion]] is given by:

:<math> m\ddot{x} + c\dot{x} + kx = 0 </math>.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rahman |first1=J. |last2=Mushtaq |first2=M. |last3=Ali |first3=A. |last4=Anjam |first4=Y.N |last5=Nazir |first5=S. |date=2014 |title=Modelling damped mass spring system in MATHLAB Simulink |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/338158709 |journal=Journal of Faculty of Engineering & Technology |volume=2}}</ref>

The corresponding critical damping coefficient is: <math> c_c = 2 \sqrt{k m} </math>

and the [[natural frequency]] of the system is: <math> \omega_n = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} </math>

Using these definitions, the equation of motion can then be expressed as:

:<math> \ddot{x} + 2\zeta\omega_n\dot{x} + \omega_n^2 x = 0. </math>

This equation is more general than just the mass-spring-damper system and applies to electrical circuits and to other domains.  It can be solved with the approach
:<math> x(t) = C e^{s t},</math>

where ''C'' and ''s'' are both [[complex number|complex]] constants, with ''s'' satisfying
:<math> s = -\omega_n \left(\zeta \pm i \sqrt{1 - \zeta^2}\right). </math>

Two such solutions, for the two values of ''s'' satisfying the equation, can be combined to make the general real solutions, with oscillatory and decaying properties in several regimes:
[[File:Phase_portrait_of_damped_oscillator,_with_increasing_damping_strength.gif|thumb|Phase portrait of damped oscillator, with increasing damping strength. It starts at undamped, proceeds to underdamped, then critically damped, then overdamped.]]
; Undamped: Is the case where <math>\zeta = 0</math> corresponds to the undamped simple harmonic oscillator, and in that case the solution looks like <math>\exp(i\omega_nt)</math>, as expected. This case is extremely rare in the natural world with the closest examples being cases where friction was purposefully reduced to minimal values.
; Underdamped: If ''s'' is a pair of complex values, then each complex solution term is a decaying exponential combined with an oscillatory portion that looks like <math display="inline">\exp\left(i \omega_n \sqrt{1 - \zeta^2}t\right)</math>.  This case occurs for <math> \ 0 \le \zeta < 1 </math>, and is referred to as ''underdamped'' (e.g., bungee cable).
; Overdamped: If ''s'' is a pair of real values, then the solution is simply a sum of two decaying exponentials with no oscillation. This case occurs for <math> \zeta > 1 </math>, and is referred to as ''overdamped''. Situations where overdamping is practical tend to have tragic outcomes if overshooting occurs, usually electrical rather than mechanical. For example, landing a plane in autopilot: if the system overshoots and releases landing gear too late, the outcome would be a disaster.
; Critically damped: The case where <math> \zeta = 1 </math> is the border between the overdamped and underdamped cases, and is referred to as ''critically damped''. This turns out to be a desirable outcome in many cases where engineering design of a damped oscillator is required (e.g., a door closing mechanism).

== ''Q'' factor and decay rate ==
The [[Q factor|''Q'' factor]], damping ratio ''ζ'', and exponential decay rate α are related such that<ref name=Siebert>{{cite book | title = Circuits, Signals, and Systems | author = William McC. Siebert | publisher = MIT Press }}</ref>
:<math>
\zeta = \frac{1}{2 Q} = { \alpha \over \omega_n }.
</math>

When a second-order system has <math>\zeta < 1</math> (that is, when the system is underdamped), it has two [[complex conjugate]] poles that each have a [[real part]] of <math>-\alpha</math>; that is, the decay rate parameter represents the rate of [[exponential decay]] of the oscillations. A lower damping ratio implies a lower decay rate, and so very underdamped systems oscillate for long times.<ref>
{{cite book
 | title = Process control engineering: a textbook for chemical, mechanical and electrical engineers
 | author = Ming Rao and Haiming Qiu
 | publisher = CRC Press
 | year = 1993
 | isbn = 978-2-88124-628-9
 | page = 96
 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=NOpmEHNRH98C&pg=PA96
 }}</ref>  For example, a high quality [[tuning fork]], which has a very low damping ratio, has an oscillation that lasts a long time, decaying very slowly after being struck by a hammer.

==Logarithmic decrement==

[[File:Dampingratio111.svg|thumb|400px|right]]

For underdamped vibrations, the damping ratio is also related to the [[logarithmic decrement]] <math>\delta</math>. The damping ratio can be found for any two peaks, even if they are not adjacent.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.brown.edu/Departments/Engineering/Courses/En4/Notes/vibrations_free_damped/vibrations_free_damped.htm|title = Dynamics and Vibrations: Notes: Free Damped Vibrations}}</ref>  For adjacent peaks:<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://pm-engr.com/damping-evaluation-2/|title = Damping Evaluation|date = 19 October 2015}}</ref>
 
:<math> \zeta = \frac{\delta}{\sqrt{\delta^2 + \left(2\pi\right)^2}}</math>  where <math>\delta = \ln\frac{x_0}{x_1}</math>

where ''x''<sub>0</sub> and ''x''<sub>1</sub> are amplitudes of any two successive peaks.

As shown in the right figure:

:<math>  \delta = \ln\frac{x_1}{x_3}=\ln\frac{x_2}{x_4}=\ln\frac{x_1-x_2}{x_3-x_4}</math>

where <math>x_1</math>, <math>x_3</math> are amplitudes of two successive positive peaks and <math>x_2</math>, <math>x_4</math> are amplitudes of two successive negative peaks.

== Percentage overshoot ==
In [[control theory]], [[Overshoot (signal)|overshoot]] refers to an output exceeding its final, steady-state value.<ref name="Kuo">{{cite book|url=http://worldcat.org/isbn/0471134767|title=Automatic control systems|author=Kuo, Benjamin C & Golnaraghi M F|publisher=Wiley|year=2003|isbn=0-471-13476-7|edition=Eighth|location=NY|page=§7.3 p. 236–237}}</ref>  For a [[Step response|step input]], the '''percentage overshoot''' (PO) is the maximum value minus the step value divided by the step value. In the case of the unit step, the ''overshoot'' is just the maximum value of the step response minus one.

The percentage overshoot (PO) is related to damping ratio (''ζ'') by:

: <math> \mathrm{PO} = 100 \exp \left({-\frac{\zeta\pi}{\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}}}\right) </math>

Conversely, the damping ratio (''ζ'') that yields a given percentage overshoot is given by:

: <math> \zeta = \frac{-\ln\left(\frac{\rm PO}{100}\right)}{\sqrt{\pi^2 + \ln^2\left(\frac{\rm PO}{100}\right)}} </math>

== Examples and applications ==

=== Viscous drag ===
{{main|Viscous damping|Dashpot}}

When an object is falling through the air, the only force opposing its freefall is air resistance. An object falling through water or oil would slow down at a greater rate, until eventually reaching a steady-state velocity as the drag force comes into equilibrium with the force from gravity. This is the concept of [[Drag (physics)|viscous drag]], which for example is applied in automatic doors or anti-slam doors.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=damping {{!}} Definition, Types, & Examples|url=https://www.britannica.com/science/damping|access-date=2021-06-09|website=Encyclopedia Britannica|language=en}}</ref>

=== Damping in electrical systems ===
Electrical systems that operate with [[alternating current]] (AC) use resistors to damp LC resonant circuits.<ref name=":0" />

=== Magnetic damping ===
{{main|Magnetic damping}}

Kinetic energy that causes oscillations is dissipated as heat by electric [[eddy current]]s which are induced by passing through a magnet's poles, either by a coil or aluminum plate. Eddy currents are a key component of [[electromagnetic induction]] where they set up a [[magnetic flux]] directly opposing the oscillating movement, creating a resistive force.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Gupta |first=B. R. |title=Principles of Electrical, Electronics and Instrumentation Engineering |publisher=S. chand Limited |year=2001 |isbn=9788121901031 |pages=338 |language=English}}</ref> In other words, the resistance caused by magnetic forces slows a system down. An example of this concept being applied is the [[Eddy current brake|brakes]] on roller coasters.

=== Magnetorheological damping ===
{{main|Magnetorheological damper}}

Magnetorheological dampers (MR Dampers) use [[Magnetorheological fluid]], which changes viscosity when subjected to a magnetic field. In this case, Magnetorheological damping may be considered an interdisciplinary form of damping with both viscous and magnetic damping mechanisms.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=LEE |first1=DUG-YOUNG |last2=WERELEY |first2=NORMAN M. |title=Quasi-Steady Herschel-Bulkley Analysis of Electro- and Magneto-Rheological Flow Mode Dampers |date=June 2000 |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1142/9789812793607_0066 |journal=Electro-Rheological Fluids and Magneto-Rheological Suspensions |pages=579–586 |publisher=WORLD SCIENTIFIC |doi=10.1142/9789812793607_0066|isbn=978-981-02-4258-9 |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last1=Savaresi |first1=Sergio M. |chapter=CHAPTER 2 - Semi-Active Suspension Technologies and Models |date=2010-01-01 |chapter-url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B978008096678600002X |title=Semi-Active Suspension Control Design for Vehicles |pages=15–39 |editor-last=Savaresi |editor-first=Sergio M. |access-date=2023-07-15 |place=Boston |publisher=Butterworth-Heinemann |language=en |doi=10.1016/b978-0-08-096678-6.00002-x |isbn=978-0-08-096678-6 |last2=Poussot-Vassal |first2=Charles |last3=Spelta |first3=Cristiano |last4=Sename |first4=Oliver |last5=Dugard |first5=Luc |editor2-last=Poussot-Vassal |editor2-first=Charles |editor3-last=Spelta |editor3-first=Cristiano |editor4-last=Sename |editor4-first=Oliver|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref>

=== Material damping ===

Materials have varying degrees of internal damping properties due to microstructural mechanisms within them. This property is sometimes known as [[damping capacity]]. In metals, this arises due to movements of dislocations, as demonstrated nicely in this video:<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=P345p7A4IW8 | title=Bubble Raft Model - part 1 | website=[[YouTube]] | date=24 October 2016 }}</ref> metals, as well as ceramics and glass, are known for having very light material damping. By contrast, polymers have a much higher material damping that arises from the energy loss required to contiually break and reform the [[Van der Waals forces]] between polymer chains. The cross-linking in [[thermoset]] plastics causes less movement of the polymer chains and so the damping is less.

Material damping is best characterized by the loss factor <math>\eta</math>, given by the equation below for the case of very light damping, such as in metals or ceramics:

:<math>\eta = 2\zeta\frac{\omega}{\omega_n}</math>

This is because many microstructural processes that contribute to material damping are not well modelled by viscous damping, and so the damping ratio varies with frequency. Adding the frequency ratio as a factor typically makes the loss factor constant over a wide frequency range.
